metric.why: Transformer and switchgear lead times stretched from months to years and now gate construction schedules as hard as permits do. Lead-time surveys are published by industry groups and research firms; watch the directory sources.
metric.definition: Order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators.

reading.body:
Equipment lead times for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling systems, and high-end accelerators have lengthened from months to years and now constrain data center construction as severely as permitting does.

This shift marks the transition from regulatory and land-use limits to physical production constraints. When supply chains tighten enough to match the pace of bureaucracy, neither dominates alone. Both must move faster for building to accelerate. The data centers that house AI compute cannot be built faster than their most bottlenecked component can be delivered.

For AI scaling, this matters because compute growth depends on buildings, and buildings now depend on industrial capacity that cannot easily surge. A transformer ordered today may not arrive for years. This creates a hard ceiling on how many data centers can come online simultaneously, regardless of capital available or sites approved. The constraint is real and measurable but does not appear in chip counts or FLOPS projections.

The data does not show which specific equipment delays longest, how lead times vary by geography or supplier, or whether they are lengthening still or have stabilized. It flags what to watch without quantifying the gap between demand and delivery capacity.
